name: Ollama
look: One continuous paper-white sheet, pill geometry everywhere, black CTAs and an inline curl snippet as the signature element.

hero.title: Run large language models locally
hero.sub: One command to pull a model, one to run it. No API key, no account, and nothing leaves your machine.

features.title: Your machine, your models
features.sub: Everything runs on hardware you own, which changes what you are willing to paste into a prompt.

items.title: One command
items.body: `localhost pull llama3` and you are running. No key, no console, no billing page.

items.title: Nothing leaves
items.body: Prompts and outputs never touch a network. Air-gap the machine and it still works.

items.title: 180+ models
items.body: Every major open-weight family, quantised into builds that fit real hardware.

items.title: OpenAI-compatible
items.body: Drop-in endpoint, so existing code points at localhost and keeps working.

items.title: GPU when there is one
items.body: Metal, CUDA and ROCm used automatically, with a graceful CPU fallback.

items.title: Modelfiles
items.body: Pin a system prompt, parameters and adapter into one reproducible file you can commit.

showcases.title: Two commands, then you are talking to it
showcases.body: Install, pull a model, run it. The first pull downloads a quantised build sized for your hardware; after that, startup is a couple of seconds and everything is local.
points: Models cached and shared between projects

showcases.title: A drop-in replacement endpoint
showcases.body: The server speaks the OpenAI chat API, so an existing application points at localhost and works unchanged. Useful for testing prompts without spending anything, and for shipping software that must run without a network.
points: Runs as a service or in Docker

gallery.title: Model library
gallery.sub: Open-weight families, quantised and ready to pull.

testimonial.quote: I put a client contract into a prompt for the first time, because the machine was on my desk and the wifi was off. That is the entire product.
testimonial.name: Dana Whitfield

pricing.title: Pricing
pricing.sub: The runtime is free and open source, forever.

tiers.name: Max
tiers.desc: For heavy local and hosted use.

items.a: No. Smaller models run acceptably on a modern laptop CPU. A GPU is used automatically when present and makes larger models practical.

items.q: Does anything get sent to you?
items.a: No. The runtime makes no network calls except to pull a model you asked for. Verify it with a packet capture — people have.

items.q: How much disk will it use?
items.a: A 7B model in a common quantisation is roughly 4GB. Models are cached once and shared across every project on the machine.
MIT licensed, including commercial use. The paid tiers add sync and hosted capacity, not runtime features.

cta.title: Run your first model in a minute
cta.sub: Free and open source. No account, no key, no telemetry.

notes: The whole page is one continuous paper-white sheet — no surface alternation, no section shading.
Pill geometry everywhere: every button and input is fully rounded, cards are softly rounded, nothing is sharp.
A single black CTA carries every action. The pricing card variants are the only deviation.
The inline curl-style install snippet sits directly under the hero headline and is the most signature element on the page.
The dark inverted pricing card breaks the flat-white rhythm exactly once per page. Twice would ruin it.
